title: Pipkin and the Grumble-Slug Mystery
markdown:
The Whispering Peaks held villages like moss on a ledge. Rope bridges were threads against a lot of sky, and people crossed them as if the habit of not looking down were a local dialect. Pine-dark passes smelled of damp earth and old weather. Wind told stories whether anyone had asked.

Pipkin the goblin grinned often, but his fingers were usually dark with garden soil, not mischief. His plot clung to a shelf of rock and still managed colour: moonpetal, dreamweed for evenings, sparkleroot for festivals, sunsprouts that believed they were the point of autumn. He argued with the wind and mostly won, staking, muttering, offering extra water like an apology. Cog, a sturdy rat with a nervous career, wrung his paws in the doorway of the potting shed. Whiskers quivered like forks that had heard a tune and not liked the key.

“The dew is still on the cobwebs,” Cog squeaked. “The crows have not begun gossip.”

Pipkin’s nose was nearly in the bed. Dew still jewelled the cobwebs; a late moth pretended to be a petal. “A print. By the prize sunsprouts.” A mark like a tiny clawed hand, too round, too smudged. Another by the dreamweed, which had the decency to look offended. Another, deeper, as if the visitor had grown heavier while walking, or had been carrying a worry. Soil had been pushed, not kicked. His garden was a sanctuary with rules: labels, spacing, a polite fence. Unknown feet were an insult and a riddle. Pebble, the resident grumble-slug, was asleep under a pot and therefore innocent by alibi.

“A large beetle,” Cog offered. “Odd feet. Fermented berries. Hind legs for admiration.”

“Beetles do not stand to praise sunsprouts. Deliberate. The Harvest Festival is days off. The potions and pies need these herbs. I will not have peculiar marks for a centrepiece.” His stomach churned like stew that had not been introduced to a spoon.

“Investigation?” Cog imagined damp, eyes, extra legs. “My bravery is medium-sized.”

Pipkin patted a dusty head. “Resourcefulness. And you.” He did not name a theme. He went up-mountain to Sorrel the witch, whose cottage smelled of woodsmoke and burnt sugar, lavender haze, windowsill plants that blinked at clouds as if clouds were gossip.

The climb to Sorrel’s door was a conversation with switchbacks. Cog counted reasons to go home and lost count, which was progress. Smoke wrote a lazy letter on the sky. She stirred emerald brew, mint and secrets, and did not look surprised to see soil on a goblin before breakfast.

“Whispering winds? Dancing dew? The giggle-broth? Or have the snails unionised?”

“Footprints. In the herbs. Not right. Too round. Too sure of themselves.”

Stone spectacles made prisms of the light. A windowsill plant blinked, slowly, as if taking minutes. “Inconvenient for snails. They get confused by unfamiliar tracks and then they write letters of complaint in slime. Were the prints looking, or only passing? Looking leaves a different weight.”

Cog, seized by tidying, nudged a pouch. Buttons and coloured string cascaded. His ears dropped.

“Miscellaneous discoveries,” Sorrel said, not unkind. “A mind like a dandelion seed.” She lifted a lumpy button. “Grumble-slug shell, too smooth. This string is for glow-moss bundles, too tangled to work. Glimble the trader is in the square this afternoon. Unusual wares. Sometimes more unusual finds by the Whispering Falls.”

They scurried down the switchbacks, Cog’s worry thinning toward curiosity and then thickening again at a loose stone. A crow remarked. Pipkin did not translate. In the square, Glimble’s stall hummed with rocks, dream-feathers, a kettle that might have been a hat, and a smell of travel. Village voices bargained. Pipkin needed fence-twine that meant it, because the prints had made the boundary feel like a suggestion.

“Sturdy twine. The fence has seen better days and is about to see worse.”

Glimble, bulbous cheerful nose, mica eyes, produced gossamer silk. “Butterfly nets!”

“A trowel.”

A jeweled music box, abalone lid. “Exquisite little holes.”

“A watering can.”

A miniature teapot. “Dewdrop tea.”

Cog sniffed the stall’s base and found a warm grey stone with indentations—the garden prints in miniature, a cousin to Pebble, Pipkin’s own grumble-slug. It rolled, sighed like a pebble with feelings.

“Where?” Pipkin asked, pulse drumming.

“Whispering Falls. Shy. Rolled away. Nudged the wrong goods at me, bless it. Lucky charm. Or a confused pebble.”

The garden, the button, the useless trades: not mischief. A lost thing trying to shop. “Not a prophecy,” Pipkin said. “A shopping list with ambition.” The baby wanted hiding-places, drink, and had mistaken fragrant herbs for moss and safety.

A rumble moved the pass, the mountain clearing its throat. Pebbles showered, missed them by the width of a good decision, and sent them scrambling. Cog hid behind Pipkin’s legs and announced that bravery had gone to check on the shed. They ducked into an alcove velvet with moss that smelled of burrow and home, of the garden after rain. Pipkin pressed a palm to the green and felt the same comfort he tried to grow on purpose. When the last stone settled, urgency arrived properly: if a small creature was writing lists with its feet, a rockfall was a poor postscript. Glimble, now interested and carrying the teapot as if it might yet become useful, came too. The print-trail, still readable despite the tremor, led toward the Falls, where the water practised the same sentence forever.

The Falls were louder than gossip. Spray made a second weather. A small grey grumble-slug huddled at the water, shell dull, legs nervous: Glimble’s stone, unstoned, the indentations matching Pipkin’s beds as a key matches a door it has already tried. It had been trying for the garden, then the alcove, then anywhere that understood moss as a language. It nudged a second, slightly larger slug toward Pipkin: comfort, not tribute. The larger one had a chip in its shell like a comma.

“Lost,” Pipkin said, kneeling so he would not be a mountain. “And tired of teapots. We have moss that means it.” Cog, from a polite distance, confirmed the leg situation. Glimble took off his cap, which was the closest he came to theology.

Sorrel arrived, having followed the determined line from her pot. Her rare smile arrived with a polished gourd. “Not malice. Comfort, misplaced. Glimble’s wares were a language with the wrong nouns.” The gourd was for a creature that wanted a home and a drink.

They built a sheltered pocket by Pipkin’s beds, in the lee of the fence that still needed twine and would now have guests instead. Glimble emptied a sack of mosses and stones he had meant for sculptures, he said, too quickly, and arranged them as if arranging were a kind of apology. Sorrel set the gourd where rain would find it. Pipkin cut the softest herbs and did not count them as inventory. The slugs settled, one against the other, like a sentence that had found its verb. Shells remembered sheen. Cog inspected the perimeter for extra legs and, finding the usual number, sat down as if the job had been military.

The Festival did what festivals do when the herbs are right: pies, moonpetal on the tables, sparkleroot in the lanterns, laughter that did not need a moral pinned to the well. Someone praised the sunsprouts. Pipkin did not mention the prints. A shy warm shell nuzzled his hand when he went to check the pocket at dusk. Cog offered dried berry, still relieved. Glimble sold a genuine trowel the next week, as if the mountain had decided to cooperate. Pipkin left a little extra moss at the border, in case anyone small was still writing lists with their feet, and slept without inventing beetles.
characters: Pipkin (goblin Pipkin), Cog (rat Cog), Sorrel (witch Sorrel)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
